answers.plain:
Start with `/var/log`. It's the safest of the two, and you can reclaim a lot there without touching anything a build depends on. Run these on the build server itself. The shell I have access to is a local Mac, not your server.

## 1. Find out what's big (read-only)

```bash
sudo du -xh /var/log --max-depth=2 | sort -rh | head -20
sudo ls -lhS /var/log | head -20
sudo lsof +L1 2>/dev/null | grep -i deleted | head   # deleted-but-still-open files holding space
```

## 2. Clean /var/log safely

**Journald** (if systemd):
```bash
journalctl --disk-usage
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=1G     # or --vacuum-time=7d
```

**Old rotated and compressed logs.** These are already archived, so they're safe to delete:
```bash
sudo find /var/log -type f \( -name "*.gz" -o -name "*.[0-9]" -o -name "*.old" \) -mtime +7 -print     # review first
sudo find /var/log -type f \( -name "*.gz" -o -name "*.[0-9]" -o -name "*.old" \) -mtime +7 -delete
```

**A huge active log.** Don't `rm` it, because the process keeps the file handle open and the space isn't freed. Truncate it instead:
```bash
sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/<biglog>
```
If you want to keep recent content, run `sudo tail -n 10000 /var/log/<biglog> > /tmp/keep && sudo cp /tmp/keep /var/log/<biglog>` first. Truncating is a fine default if the log is just noise.

Then fix the cause. Check `logrotate` config (`/etc/logrotate.d/`) and find out why 19G piled up. It's often a debug-level logger or a crash loop.

## 3. /opt/cache: be more careful

This is the one that can break running builds if you delete something in use. First, find out what it is:
```bash
ls -lah /opt/cache
sudo du -h --max-depth=2 /opt/cache | sort -rh | head -20
```

- **Use the tool's own prune command if there is one.** For example, `docker system prune` (without `-a` at first), `gradle`/`maven`/`npm cache clean`, or `ccache -c`. These know what's in use.
- **Otherwise, delete only by age,** and only entries nobody has touched recently:
  ```bash
  sudo find /opt/cache -type f -atime +14 -print | head     # review
  sudo find /opt/cache -type f -atime +14 -delete
  ```
  If the filesystem is mounted `noatime`, use `-mtime` instead.
- **Check for active use first:** `sudo lsof +D /opt/cache | head` and look at what your CI agent is running.
- The worst case is usually a slow first build that rebuilds the cache. But don't delete the whole directory mid-build, because jobs can fail on missing files.

## 4. Verify
```bash
df -h /
```

## Suggested order
1. Journald vacuum and old rotated `.gz` logs, which should free several GB at no risk.
2. Truncate any runaway active log.
3. Age-based or tool-native pruning of `/opt/cache`, ideally between builds.

If you paste the `du` output for both directories, I can tell you more precisely what to target. Also check that something isn't still writing logs quickly, or you'll be back here in a day.
answers.nudge:
I can't reach your server from here, so this is a runbook to run yourself. Steps 0–2 are read-only. The order goes from lowest risk to highest.

## 0. Triage (read-only, 2 minutes)

```bash
df -h /; df -i /                      # check inodes too, not just blocks
sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /var/log | sort -rh | head -15
sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /opt/cache | sort -rh | head -15
sudo lsof +L1 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR==1 || $7>100000000'   # deleted files still held open by processes
```

The `lsof +L1` check matters. If a process holds a deleted log open, `df` stays full until that process closes it. That is the usual reason "I deleted it but the space didn't come back."

Also find out what is running and what is writing:

```bash
sudo find /var/log -type f -size +500M -printf '%s\t%TY-%Tm-%Td\t%p\n' | sort -rn | head
ps aux | egrep -i 'jenkins|gitlab-runner|buildkite|teamcity|gradle|docker' | grep -v egrep
```

If a single log is huge and its mtime is today, something is spamming it. Cleaning it will only buy you a few hours, so find the cause.

## 1. /var/log (19G): safest wins first

**a) Journald, if present** (safe, and it won't touch running processes):
```bash
journalctl --disk-usage
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M      # or --vacuum-time=7d
```

**b) Old rotated and compressed logs** (already rotated, so nothing is writing to them):
```bash
sudo find /var/log -type f \( -name '*.gz' -o -name '*.[0-9]' -o -name '*.old' -o -name '*.xz' \) -mtime +14 -print      # review the list
sudo find /var/log -type f \( -name '*.gz' -o -name '*.[0-9]' -o -name '*.old' -o -name '*.xz' \) -mtime +14 -delete
```

**c) Compress large rotated-but-uncompressed logs** if you want to keep them:
```bash
sudo find /var/log -type f -name '*.log.1' -size +100M -exec gzip {} \;
```

**d) A live, actively written log: truncate it, never `rm` it.** Deleting it leaves the process writing to an invisible inode and frees nothing.
```bash
sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/path/to/huge.log
```
Save the last bit first if you need it: `sudo tail -n 10000 big.log > /root/big.log.tail`.

**e) Force a logrotate pass**, then check that rotation is actually configured for the offender:
```bash
sudo logrotate -v /etc/logrotate.conf
```

## 2. /opt/cache (17G): be careful here

First identify what it is. The right cleanup depends on the tool, and a blind `rm -rf` can fail builds mid-run, either with missing artifacts or with corrupted partial caches.

```bash
ls -la /opt/cache
sudo find /opt/cache -type f -atime +30 -printf '%s\n' | awk '{s+=$1} END {printf "%.1f GB not accessed in 30d\n", s/1e9}'
sudo lsof +D /opt/cache 2>/dev/null | head      # what's open right now
```

Then use age-based deletion, so recently used entries that active builds depend on are left alone:

```bash
# dry run
sudo find /opt/cache -type f -atime +30 -print | head -50
# delete, only after reviewing
sudo find /opt/cache -type f -atime +30 -delete
sudo find /opt/cache -type d -empty -delete
```

Prefer the tool's own pruning when it exists, because it is lock-aware:
- Docker: `docker system df`, then `docker image prune -a --filter "until=168h"` and `docker builder prune --filter "until=168h"`. Don't use `--volumes` blindly.
- Gradle: `find ~/.gradle/caches -atime +30 -delete`, or the `org.gradle.cache.cleanup` setting.
- Maven, npm and pip: `npm cache clean --force`, `pip cache purge`. Maven has no built-in prune, so use age-based `find` on `~/.m2/repository`.
- ccache: `ccache --evict-older-than 14d`, or `ccache -M 5G`.
- Bazel: `bazel clean --expunge` is heavy. Prefer a disk cache GC setting.

If `atime` is mounted `noatime` or `relatime`, atime is unreliable. Use `-mtime` or check `mount | grep ' / '`.

**Avoid:** `rm -rf /opt/cache/*` while builds are active, and anything with `-mtime -N` (recent) by mistake. The cleanest approach is to do the bulk deletion when the build queue drains, or to put the agent in drain/offline mode first (for Jenkins, mark the node offline).

## 3. Expected result

Steps 1a–1d plus an age-based cache prune should typically free 10–25G, which gets you to about 60–70% used. If it doesn't, check these:
```bash
sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -rh | head      # something outside those two dirs
sudo docker system df; sudo du -sh /var/lib/docker /var/lib/apt/lists /var/cache /tmp /home 2>/dev/null
```

## 4. Prevent a repeat

- Put a size cap in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`: `SystemMaxUse=1G`.
- Add a logrotate rule with `daily`, `rotate 7`, `compress`, `maxsize 200M` for the noisy app log.
- Add a nightly cron or systemd timer for the cache prune, with the same `find -atime +N` pattern or the tool-native command.
- Alert at 80% with a trend or predictive rule, for example Prometheus `predict_linear(node_filesystem_avail_bytes[6h], 24*3600) < 0`. A static 96% alert gives you almost no lead time.
- Long term, move `/opt/cache` to its own volume. That way a runaway cache can't starve `/var/log` and the OS, and you can resize it independently.

If you paste the `du` output for the two directories (or the top offenders), I can tell you exactly which files are safe to clear and write the specific commands.
answers.skill:
# Disk cleanup plan: /dev/sda1 at 96% (46G of 48G)

This plan is written from your description. I haven't run anything, and this machine isn't your build server. Run the commands there as a user with sudo.

## Assumptions about /opt/cache
- It holds regenerable build artifacts: dependency caches (npm, pip, Maven, Gradle), compiler caches (ccache, sccache), and Docker or layer caches. Nothing in it is a source of truth.
- Running builds hold some of those files open or are about to read them. A deleted cache entry only costs a rebuild or re-download, but a file removed mid-read can fail a build. That is why step 3 excludes open files.
- Some of it may belong to a tool with its own prune command (`ccache`, `docker`, `gradle`, `npm`). If so, use that command in place of `find -delete`.
- /var/log is mostly systemd-journald plus app or build logs, with old rotations in `.gz`.

## Step 1: Read-only diagnosis (frees nothing, changes nothing)

```bash
df -h /
sudo du -xh --max-depth=2 /var/log 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -30
sudo du -xh --max-depth=2 /opt/cache 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -30
journalctl --disk-usage
sudo lsof +L1 | sort -k7 -rn | head -20          # deleted-but-open files, biggest first
sudo lsof +D /opt/cache 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR>1{print $1,$2,$3,$9}' | sort -u   # who holds what
ps -eo pid,etime,user,cmd | grep -Ei 'jenkins|gitlab-runner|buildkite|make|gradle|mvn|npm|docker build' | grep -v grep
```

- **Why it's safe:** every command only reads.
- **What it gives you:** the targets for the later steps, the active builds, and the exact paths they hold open.
- **Deleted-but-open files:** `lsof +L1` shows space that `du` can't see. If a big one appears, truncate it through `/proc/<pid>/fd/<n>` (`: > /proc/<pid>/fd/<n>`). That frees the space without restarting the process.
- **`lsof +D` may be slow:** on a 17G tree it can take a while. If it is too slow, use `sudo lsof -c <buildtool> | grep /opt/cache` per tool.

## Step 2: Logs (lowest risk, expect to free up to about 19G)

**2a. Journal vacuum**
```bash
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M
```
- **Frees:** most of the journal's share of /var/log, often several GB.
- **Why it's safe:** it removes only archived journal files. Active files and running services are untouched.

**2b. Delete only old compressed rotations (dry-run first)**
```bash
sudo find /var/log -xdev -type f \( -name '*.gz' -o -name '*.xz' -o -name '*.[0-9]' \) -mtime +14 -print
sudo find /var/log -xdev -type f \( -name '*.gz' -o -name '*.xz' -o -name '*.[0-9]' \) -mtime +14 -delete
```
- **Frees:** old rotated logs.
- **Why it's safe:** rotated files aren't written to. Check the dry-run list first; if you need audit retention, keep `/var/log/audit`.

**2c. Forced logrotate**
```bash
sudo logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.conf
```
- **Frees:** nothing until the rotated files are compressed or deleted. It moves live logs aside, so the next vacuum or delete can reclaim them.
- **Why it's safe:** logrotate signals or reopens the logs through each service's configured postrotate hook.
- **Caveat:** a service without a reopen hook keeps writing to the rotated file. If `lsof +L1` shows that afterwards, use 2d.

**2d. Truncate oversized logs a live process holds open (never `rm`)**
```bash
sudo ls -lhS /var/log | head
sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/<oversized>.log
```
- **Frees:** the full size of that file immediately.
- **Why it's safe:** truncating keeps the inode, so the writer's file descriptor stays valid. `rm` would leave the space allocated until the process exits.
- **Cost:** you lose that log's contents. Copy off anything you need first.

## Step 3: Cache (expect to free up to about 17G)

**3a. Dry-run: files not accessed in 14+ days, excluding open ones**
```bash
sudo lsof -F n +D /opt/cache 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^n//p' | sort -u > /tmp/open_files.txt
sudo find /opt/cache -xdev -type f -atime +14 -print | sort | grep -vxFf /tmp/open_files.txt > /tmp/cache_candidates.txt
wc -l /tmp/cache_candidates.txt
xargs -a /tmp/cache_candidates.txt -d '\n' du -ch 2>/dev/null | tail -1
```
- **Why it's safe:** it only lists files and writes two scratch files in /tmp.
- **Check before step 3b:** if the volume is mounted `noatime`, `-atime` is unreliable. Run `mount | grep ' / '`. If you see `noatime`, switch to `-mtime +14`. On `relatime`, atime is good enough.

**3b. Delete the reviewed list**
```bash
xargs -a /tmp/cache_candidates.txt -d '\n' sudo rm -f --
sudo find /opt/cache -xdev -type d -empty -mindepth 1 -delete
```
- **Why it's safe:** it removes only the reviewed files, which are 14+ days idle and not open. A build that wants one later regenerates it.
- **Why a list file rather than `find -delete`:** the exclusion set is fixed at review time, so what you reviewed is what gets deleted.
- **Race:** a build could open a listed file between the review and the delete. The risk is low for 14-day-idle files. Run 3a and 3b close together.

**3c. If a tool owns the cache, use its prune instead of 3b**
```bash
ccache --evict-older-than 14d     # or: ccache -M 5G
docker builder prune --filter until=336h
npm cache clean --force           # only if no npm builds are active
gradle: delete ~/.gradle/caches only when no daemons are running
```
Each of these knows its own locking and is safer than raw `find`. Run them as the user that owns the cache.

## Step 4: Verify

```bash
df -h /                                           # compare with the Step 1 reading
sudo lsof +L1 | head                              # should be empty or tiny
ps -eo pid,etime,cmd | grep -Ei 'gradle|mvn|npm|make|runner' | grep -v grep   # same PIDs, etimes still increasing
tail -n 20 <active build log>                     # output still advancing
```
Then trigger or wait for the next build. A pass confirms the cache loss is only a slower, cold-cache run. Aim for 70% or less used. If you are still above 85%, stop and send the Step 1 output instead of deleting more.

## Step 5: Prevention

| Folder | What let it grow | One-line fix |
|---|---|---|
| /var/log (journal) | No size cap on journald | `SystemMaxUse=1G` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`, then `sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald` |
| /var/log (app logs) | No rotation limit or missing `rotate N` | In the app's `/etc/logrotate.d/` file: `rotate 7`, `daily`, `compress`, `maxsize 200M` |
| /opt/cache | No eviction, so every build adds and nothing leaves | Cron: `0 3 * * * find /opt/cache -xdev -type f -atime +14 -delete` (or the tool's own prune, such as `ccache -M 5G`) |

Add a disk alert at 80% as well, so you catch this before it reaches 96%.

## Paste back

Paste the output of this command from Step 1:

```bash
sudo du -xh --max-depth=2 /var/log /opt/cache 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -40
```

With that listing I can name the exact files and subdirectories to clean and pick the right prune command for the cache.
